title: Dry-run: modeling a social graph on a normal database

spec.title: Dry-run: modeling a social graph on a normal database
spec.intro: About 5 minutes. No graph database here — the point is showing an adjacency list works fine until one specific query stops scaling.

steps.title: The edge table is the whole schema
steps.explain: A follow graph is just directed edges: who follows whom. Storing it as rows rather than an array on the user row is what makes 'who follows me' and 'who do I follow' both single indexed lookups instead of a scan.

steps.title: One-hop queries are cheap in both directions
steps.explain: This is the entire reason to index both columns: 'who do I follow' hits the primary key, 'who follows me' hits the secondary index, and neither one touches a row it doesn't need.

steps.title: Mutual friends: still one hop each side
steps.explain: A two-set intersection of one-hop queries covers 'friends in common,' which is the query people actually mean by 'graph query' most of the time — no traversal engine required.

steps.title: Second-degree — where the naive version breaks
steps.explain: Friend-of-friend looks like just one more hop, but naively it means N+1 queries — one to get your friends, then one per friend to get theirs. At a few hundred friends this is a request storm against the database.

steps.title: Fix: one join instead of N round trips
steps.explain: Pushing the second hop into the database as a join collapses N round trips into one, and lets the query planner use the index instead of the application looping over network calls.
steps.saysOutLoud: The fix isn't a different data model, it's doing the hop where the index lives.

steps.title: Beyond two hops, stop doing this in the primary store
steps.explain: Three-plus hop traversals (recommendation-style 'people you may know') fan out combinatorially and a relational join stops being viable. That workload moves to a dedicated graph engine (Neo4j) or a precomputed nightly batch job that materializes candidate results — the edge table stays the source of truth, the traversal store is a derived cache.

steps.title: A celebrity account skews the whole shape
steps.explain: The one-hop queries above assume follower counts in the hundreds. An account with millions of followers turns 'who follows me' into a query returning millions of rows, and the join in step 5 becomes enormous for anyone who follows one. Cap and paginate rather than assuming any hop is bounded.

spec.closing: If they ask why not a graph database from the start: relational joins handle one and two hops fine at a fraction of the operational cost, and most social-graph queries in practice are one hop — reach for a graph engine only once traversal depth actually demands it.
